title: Announces U.S. Will Not Join the Arms Trade Treaty
description_medium: At the National Rifle Association’s April 26, 2019 meeting, President Donald Trump said the United States would not ratify the United Nations Arms Trade Treaty and asked the Senate to return it. The United States had signed the treaty in 2013 but never ratified it. Trump cited sovereignty and Second Amendment concerns; the announcement began a formal withdrawal of the pending treaty from Senate consideration.
description_long:
Trump made the announcement while addressing the NRA’s annual meeting in Indianapolis. He described the United Nations Arms Trade Treaty as a threat to U.S. sovereignty and gun rights, and said it could constrain American arms exports. The 2013 treaty sets international standards for conventional-weapons transfers. The United States had signed it under President Barack Obama, but the Senate had not ratified it, so the country had not become a party to the treaty.

On April 26, 2019, Trump announced that he would not ratify the agreement and signed a message asking the Senate to return the treaty. He sent that formal message on April 29, stating that joining was not in the national interest. The distinction matters: this action withdrew the treaty from the Senate’s pending consideration and reversed the prior administration’s effort to secure ratification; it did not withdraw the United States from a treaty it had joined. The White House argued that existing U.S. export controls were sufficient and that the treaty could be used to challenge lawful arms sales. The NRA had opposed the agreement, while supporters viewed it as a tool to regulate international weapons transfers.

corrected_wording.original: Announces Withdrawal from the Arms Trade Treaty
corrected_wording.replacement: Announces U.S. Will Not Join the Arms Trade Treaty
corrected_wording.reason: The United States had signed but never ratified the treaty; the April 2019 action withdrew it from Senate consideration rather than ending membership.

source_access_notes: Read the archived White House April 26 statement and April 29 message to the Senate. PBS/AP same-day coverage contextualizes the NRA announcement and notes the treaty had not been ratified.
rationale: The White House statements establish the announcement, formal Senate request and administration’s stated rationale; same-day coverage clarifies that the U.S. had signed but not ratified the treaty.

title: Announces DNI Dan Coats Will Leave Office
description_medium: President Donald Trump announced in late July 2019 that Director of National Intelligence Dan Coats would leave office on August 15 and said he planned to nominate Representative John Ratcliffe as his successor. Coats had publicly differed with Trump on Russian election interference, Iran and North Korea. The departure shifted leadership of the intelligence community during disputes over how its assessments were presented.
description_long:
Trump announced Coats’s departure on July 28, 2019, saying he would leave on August 15 and that the president planned to nominate Texas Representative John Ratcliffe as the next director of national intelligence. Coats submitted a resignation letter that day, describing his service as a privilege and saying it was time for a new chapter. The announcement came after a turbulent relationship marked by repeated public disagreements over intelligence findings and foreign policy.

The sharpest dispute concerned Russian interference in the 2016 election. Coats and the intelligence community maintained that Russia had interfered and continued trying to influence U.S. politics, while Trump repeatedly questioned those assessments. Coats also testified that North Korea was unlikely to give up its nuclear weapons and that Iran remained in compliance with the nuclear agreement—positions that conflicted with the president’s public claims. Coats’s departure therefore raised questions about whether the country’s top intelligence official could present conclusions that contradicted the president. Ratcliffe’s initial nomination faltered amid questions about his experience, and Coats left office on August 15; deputy director Sue Gordon served as acting director briefly before stepping down.
source_access_notes: Read ODNI’s July 28 resignation notice and contemporaneous Roll Call, Washington Post and Guardian/AP reports on the announcement, policy disagreements and succession.
rationale: ODNI confirms the resignation date and effective date; contemporaneous reporting documents the public policy disputes and the initially announced successor.

title: Pardons Angela Stanton
description_medium: On February 18, 2020, President Donald Trump granted Angela Ronae Stanton a full pardon. Stanton had been convicted in federal court in Georgia for her role in a stolen-vehicle ring and served six months of home confinement. The White House cited her later work as an author, television personality and criminal-justice reform advocate, particularly her efforts to improve reentry for people returning from prison.
description_long:
The Justice Department’s clemency record identifies Stanton’s federal case in the Northern District of Georgia. It lists a 2007 conviction for conspiracy involving interstate transportation of a stolen motor vehicle and tampering with a vehicle identification number. Her sentence was time served and three years of supervised release, including six months of home confinement. The record does not describe the full scope of her conduct in the vehicle ring.

Trump granted Stanton a full pardon on February 18, 2020, alongside six other pardons and four commutations. The distinction is significant: Stanton received a pardon, while several other people announced that day had prison terms shortened. The White House presented Stanton’s post-conviction work as its rationale, describing her as an author and television personality who advocated criminal-justice reform and worked to improve reentry for people leaving prison. It also identified Alveda King as a supporter of the grant. The clemency announcement did not claim that Stanton’s conviction was mistaken; it framed the pardon as recognition of her later rehabilitation and community work.
source_access_notes: Read Stanton’s DOJ pardon instrument and the archived White House announcement, which names the full pardon, sentence, rehabilitation rationale and supporter.
rationale: DOJ establishes the offense and sentence; the White House supplies the stated reasons for clemency and distinguishes Stanton’s full pardon from same-day commutations.

title: Fires Intelligence Community Inspector General
description_medium: On April 3, 2020, President Donald Trump notified Congress that he intended to remove Intelligence Community Inspector General Michael Atkinson, who had reviewed and transmitted the Ukraine whistleblower complaint that led to Trump’s first impeachment inquiry. Trump cited a loss of confidence but gave no detailed reason in his letter. Atkinson was placed on administrative leave before the 30-day notice period ended.
description_long:
Atkinson was the intelligence community’s independent watchdog when he received a whistleblower complaint in August 2019 about Trump’s dealings with Ukraine. He judged it credible and urgent and sought to have it sent to Congress under the whistleblower law. The complaint became central to the House’s first impeachment inquiry; the Senate acquitted Trump in February 2020.

On April 3, Trump informed the House and Senate intelligence committees that he intended to remove Atkinson in 30 days, saying he no longer had “the fullest confidence” in him. Atkinson was placed on paid administrative leave immediately, effectively ending his work before the notice period elapsed. Trump later called him a disgrace and said he had done a terrible job. Atkinson said he believed the decision stemmed from his faithful handling of the complaint. Democratic senators and watchdog advocates challenged the adequacy of the explanation, pointing out that the Inspector General Reform Act required advance written reasons for a removal. The episode intensified concerns about whether inspectors general could independently act on whistleblower disclosures involving the president.
source_access_notes: Read the Guardian’s same-event report, the senators’ April 8 letter on statutory notice requirements and Atkinson’s post-removal statement as reported by the Washington Post. The packet’s Guardian URL was a dead path; the current Guardian report was found at its corrected same-event URL.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting explains Atkinson’s role, Trump’s stated loss of confidence and Atkinson’s response; the Senate letter documents the statutory notice dispute.

title: Fires State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
description_medium: President Donald Trump announced Steve Linick’s removal as State Department inspector general on May 15, 2020, after Secretary of State Mike Pompeo recommended it. Linick’s office was examining Pompeo’s role in an emergency Saudi arms sale and allegations that a staffer handled personal errands for him and his wife. Trump and Pompeo denied retaliation; lawmakers questioned the timing and opened inquiries.
description_long:
Linick had served as State Department inspector general since 2013, overseeing investigations into agency conduct and management. On May 15, 2020, Trump notified Congress that he was removing Linick, saying he no longer had full confidence in his ability to help federal programs operate effectively. Pompeo later confirmed that he had asked Trump to fire Linick, saying Linick was undermining the department’s mission. Linick’s final day was set for June 14.

The timing drew scrutiny because Linick’s office was investigating two matters involving Pompeo: a congressionally requested review of the administration’s 2019 emergency declaration used to bypass Congress on an arms package for Saudi Arabia and other countries, and allegations that a political appointee ran personal errands for Pompeo and his wife. House Foreign Affairs Chairman Eliot Engel said the arms-sale inquiry might be another reason for the firing and called the timing troubling. Pompeo said he did not know of the investigations and denied retaliation; Trump also said he had not known about the inquiry. The State Department did not confirm specific investigations. The firings prompted congressional investigations into whether removing an inspector general during pending oversight work could chill independent watchdogs.
source_access_notes: Read CBS News and ABC News contemporaneous reports, then the Washington Post interview with Pompeo. The packet’s USA Today link was unrelated; these same-event reports establish the removal, Pompeo’s request, the pending inquiries and competing explanations.
rationale: Reporting establishes the removal and Pompeo’s request while attributing the pending investigations and retaliation allegations to lawmakers; Pompeo and Trump denied retaliatory intent.
